title: ONAN’S SIN: Was God Really Judging Masturbation—or Something Else?
paragraphs:
ONAN’S SIN: Was God Really Judging Masturbation—or Something Else?
One of the Bible’s Most Misquoted Sexual Stories Is More Disturbing Than You Think—Because Onan’s Real Sin Wasn’t Simply What Happened to His Seed. It Was What Was Happening in His Heart.
There are Bible stories people think they know because they have heard one interpretation repeated for years.
Then one day, they actually read the text.
Slowly.
In context.
And suddenly the story becomes far more uncomfortable.
Genesis 38 contains one of those moments.
For generations, the name “Onan” has become so closely associated with masturbation that the English word onanism eventually came to be associated with masturbation and related sexual practices.
So many Christians approach Genesis 38 already believing they know what happens.
Onan spills his seed.
God kills Onan.
Therefore, the argument goes, God killed Onan for masturbating.
Simple.
Except there is a serious problem.
That is not actually what Genesis says happened.
And once you see what the Hebrew text emphasizes, the story becomes much deeper than a debate about one sexual act.
It becomes a story about a man who wanted intimacy without responsibility.
Pleasure without sacrifice.
A woman without accepting the obligation he owed her.
The privileges of his position without the cost of faithfulness.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story can still make modern hearts uncomfortable.
Because Onan is easier to condemn when we reduce his story to something he did with his body.
It becomes much harder when Scripture forces us to look at what he was doing with another human being.
The story begins with death.
Judah's firstborn son, Er, had married a woman named Tamar. Genesis tells us that Er was wicked before the LORD, and he died.
Tamar was left a widow.
Then Judah told his second son, Onan, to fulfill his obligation toward her:
"וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ"
veyabbēm ʾōtāh vehāqēm zeraʿ leʾāḥîkā
In context: perform the duty of a brother-in-law toward her and “raise up offspring for your brother.”
That word matters.
זֶרַע — zeraʿ
It can mean “seed,” but in this context it means offspring or descendants.
And Scripture immediately tells us exactly what Onan understood.
"וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע"
Vayyēdaʿ ʾÔnān kî lō-lô yihyeh hazzāraʿ.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
That sentence unlocks the passage.
Onan understood the responsibility.
He understood what was expected.
He understood that a child resulting from this union would preserve his dead brother's line.
And he did not want that.
Yet notice something extraordinarily important.
Onan did not simply refuse Tamar.
He continued going to her.
Genesis 38:9 describes what happened when he had sexual relations with his brother's wife:
"וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה"
veshiḥēt ʾartṣāh
Literally, he “destroyed” or “wasted” it toward the ground.
But Scripture then supplies the purpose behind his action:
"לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו"
leviltî netan-zeraʿ leʾāḥîw
“So as not to give offspring to his brother.”
Do not rush past those words.
So as not to.
The narrator does not leave us guessing about Onan's motive.
This was deliberate.
Repeated.
Calculated.

Genesis describes him having intercourse with Tamar and deliberately preventing conception because he did not want to produce offspring for his dead brother. The text therefore does not describe masturbation as such. It describes interrupted intercourse performed specifically to frustrate the obligation Judah had commanded him to fulfill.
And then comes the terrifying sentence:
"וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה"
Vayyēraʿ beʿênê YHWH ʾăšer ʿāśāh.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
And God put him to death.
But here is where responsible Bible reading matters.
Genesis does not say:
“Onan masturbated, and therefore God killed him.”
Nor should we rewrite the verse to make it say that.
Onan was actually having intercourse with Tamar.
The text explicitly tells us why he spilled his semen: he intended to prevent the offspring from being reckoned to his deceased brother.

Later Mosaic legislation helps us understand the cultural world behind this obligation. Deuteronomy 25:5–10 describes the duty of a surviving brother toward the childless widow of his deceased brother. The purpose included preserving the deceased brother's name in Israel. A man who refused could publicly decline, but that refusal brought a formal procedure and public disgrace.
Genesis 38 occurs before that Mosaic legislation was given, so we should not carelessly pretend Onan was violating the later written statute word-for-word.
But the family obligation behind what would later be called levirate marriage is plainly present.
Judah tells him what he must do.
Onan understands.
Then Onan deliberately frustrates it.
And that makes what happened to Tamar particularly disturbing.
She had already buried her husband.
Her future was precarious.
Her place within Judah's family depended heavily upon the very household that was now failing her.
Onan apparently accepted sexual access to Tamar while deliberately refusing the offspring-producing responsibility attached to that relationship.
Think about that.
He wanted what Tamar's body could give him while refusing what faithfulness required of him.
He participated physically while withholding covenantal responsibility.
This was not merely uncontrolled desire.
There was calculation in it.
And suddenly Genesis 38 stops sounding like an obscure ancient argument about semen.
It starts sounding frighteningly modern.
Because humanity still wants pleasure without responsibility.
We still want intimacy without covenant.
Sex without holiness.
Promises without sacrifice.
Christianity without repentance.
Grace without surrender.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
We want the benefits of belonging to Christ while secretly negotiating which rooms of our lives He is permitted to enter.
And sometimes we become experts at appearing obedient while quietly engineering outcomes that serve ourselves.
Onan looked as though he was fulfilling the obligation.
He went to Tamar.
But behind the visible act was an invisible refusal.
Other people could see his body participating.
God could see his motive resisting.
That should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because you can look obedient while your heart is saying no.
You can sing worship songs while protecting a secret addiction.
You can post Scripture while refusing to forgive someone.
You can attend church while feeding lust all week.
You can speak about purity while treating another person's body as something existing for your gratification.
You can preach grace while refusing repentance.
You can call Jesus “Lord” while continually telling Him:
“Everything except this.”
And eventually Christianity reaches that locked door.
Not because Christ is cruel.
Because Christ loves us too much to pretend slavery is freedom.
Now someone will immediately ask the obvious question.
“So does that mean masturbation is fine?”
No.
It means Genesis 38 should not be made to say something it does not explicitly say.
That is different.
A Christian sexual ethic cannot be built honestly by taking Onan's story out of context.
But neither can Christian sexual ethics be reduced to the question, “Where does the Bible explicitly mention this exact modern behavior?”
Jesus takes us deeper than technical loopholes.
He goes after the heart.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus moves beyond merely avoiding the physical act of adultery and confronts lustful intention.
That changes the question.
The Christian cannot merely ask:
“Can I technically get away with this?”
The disciple of Jesus asks:
“What is forming my heart?”
“Where is my imagination going?”
“Am I learning self-control or becoming controlled?”
“Am I reducing another human being—real or imagined—to an instrument for my gratification?”
“Can I bring this before Christ without hiding?”
“Is this helping me love God and people more faithfully, or teaching me to consume people privately?”
Those questions are harder.
But holiness has never been about discovering the largest amount of darkness we can retain while still calling ourselves Christians.
Holiness is learning to love the Light.
And maybe this is where someone reading needs to stop pretending.
Maybe your struggle isn't Onan's struggle.
Maybe yours is pornography.
Maybe it is compulsive masturbation bound tightly to pornography and fantasy.
Maybe it is adultery.
Maybe sexting.
Maybe an emotional affair nobody knows about.
Maybe you have spent years feeding fantasies involving people who would be devastated if they knew how you were imagining them.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story from your Sunday worship.
Maybe you have promised God twenty times:
“Never again.”
And then you fell again.
Now shame whispers:
“Don't go back to Jesus this time.”
Listen carefully.
That voice is lying to you.
The Gospel is not the announcement that clean people can approach Christ.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can.
Jesus Christ did not shed His blood because your sin was small.
He shed His blood because your need for mercy was enormous.
Scripture does not tell sinners to hide until they become worthy.
It tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
Confession is not telling God something He doesn't know.
It is finally refusing to hide what He already sees.
That is where grace becomes breathtaking.
God sees the thing you desperately hope nobody discovers.
He sees what happened at 2:13 in the morning.
He sees the deleted history.
The second account.
The fantasy.
The relapse.
The compromise.
The secret relationship.
The hypocrisy.
He sees everything.
And the same Christ who exposes darkness stretches scarred hands toward sinners.
Not to baptize our chains.
To break them.
Not to tell us sin doesn't matter.
To forgive us and transform us.
This is where Christian grace differs radically from cheap permission.
Grace does not say:
“Stay exactly where sin left you.”
Grace says:
“Come out of the grave.”
Repentance is not purchasing God's forgiveness by becoming good enough.
Repentance is turning toward the Savior because you finally realize your sin cannot save you.
You may fall while learning to walk.
You may need accountability.
You may need to remove access.
You may need to confess to a mature believer.
You may need to stop calling something “a struggle” when you have quietly arranged your life so that you can keep feeding it.
But do not confuse warfare with abandonment.
A believer fighting sin may have scars.
The question is whether you are making peace with the enemy or running again toward Christ.
And there is another extraordinary twist in Genesis 38.
Onan's failure is not the end of Tamar's story.
Judah also fails her.
Tamar's story becomes messy, painful, morally complicated, and scandalous.
Yet God is not finished.
Read Matthew's genealogy of Jesus Christ.
There she is.
Tamar.
Matthew 1:3 names Perez and Zerah by Tamar in the genealogy that ultimately leads to Jesus.
Let that sink in.
The woman standing inside one of Genesis' most uncomfortable family scandals appears in the lineage through which Scripture traces the Messiah.
Human failure did not derail God's redemptive purpose.
The scandal did not get the final word.
Grace did.
And that does not mean God approved everything everyone did in Genesis 38.
It means human sin could not prevent God from carrying His redemptive plan forward.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Human beings bring sin.
God brings redemption.
We bring ruins.
Christ raises the dead.
We bring shame into hiding.
Christ brings sinners into the light.
We bring stories we wish could be erased.
Jesus writes resurrection across pages we thought were permanently ruined.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why you needed this story today.
You came wondering whether Onan was killed for masturbation.
But perhaps Scripture has brought you somewhere more personal.
Not:
“What exactly was Onan allowed to do?”
But:
“What am I hiding from Jesus?”
That question may matter far more.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
Let those words become a confession instead of another performance.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting battles nobody sees.
And if you are exhausted and need believers to pray for you, simply write:
No details required.
No pretending required.
Just honesty.
Send it privately to the believer who has been struggling.
But Christians can glorify God through generous, willing support of faithful Gospel work when that support flows freely from love rather than spiritual pressure.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the person who hasn't opened a Bible in years.
Invite the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing to say except condemnation.
Because the Christian message is not merely:
“Look how terrible sin is.”
It is:
Look how magnificent the Savior is.
Onan's story warns us that God sees beyond religious appearances into motives, selfishness, exploitation, and hidden rebellion.
Tamar's story reminds us that scandal does not have sovereign authority over the future.
And Jesus Christ shows us what redemption ultimately looks like.
Not sin excused.
Sin carried to a cross.
Not sinners abandoned.
Sinners called home.
Not darkness renamed as light.
Darkness invaded by Light Himself.
So tonight, when shame tells you to hide...
remember Eden.
Humanity hid.
God came looking.
Remember Peter.
He failed spectacularly.
Jesus restored him.
Remember the cross.
A criminal dying beside Jesus had nothing left to offer Him except desperate faith.
And Christ still opened Paradise.
Your darkest chapter does not have greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive His mercy.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Onan's story is not that God saw what happened on the ground.
It is that God saw what happened in the heart.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about the Gospel is this:
Jesus sees what is hiding in your heart too—and He is still calling you out of the darkness and into His grace.
